food.text: The early inhabitants of Ethiopia began domesticating grains during the Chalcolithic Age (6200-3000 BC). Plough-based agriculture may imply that cattle were domesticated around the same time. By 3000 BC, cattle, sheep, goats and donkeys were all being domesticated.
The early inhabitants of Ethiopia began domesticating grains during the Chalcolithic Age, which lasted from 6200 to 3000 BC. Farming there had deep roots thousands of years before written history.
By the Early Bronze Age, around 3000 BC, animals such as cattle, sheep, goats, and donkeys were being domesticated in Ethiopia. Herds became a new source of food alongside cultivated crops.
Handoga, a site in Djibouti dated to the fourth millennium BCE, has yielded obsidian microliths and plain ceramics. They were used by early nomadic pastoralists who kept domesticated cattle.

art.text: Dhambalin is a sandstone rock shelter in Somaliland's central Sahil province, discovered by residents of Beenyo Dhaadheer in 2007. Its multi-layered paintings, dated to about 5000 years ago, show horned cattle, goats, giraffes and the earliest known pictures of sheep in Somaliland.

Laas Geel, cave formations near Hargeisa in Somaliland, contain some of the earliest known cave paintings of domesticated African aurochs in the Horn of Africa. The rock art is estimated to be about 5,500 to 4,500 years old and spreads across ten rock alcoves in excellent condition.

The area of Somaliland was inhabited around 10,000 years ago during the Neolithic age, when ancient shepherds raised cows and other livestock and created vibrant rock art paintings. During the Stone Age, the Doian and Hargeisan cultures flourished in the region.

In the Hararghe region and Eritrea, rock paintings of human and animal figures illustrate the domestication of cattle and the crafting of pottery, hand axes, hoes and grinding stones. Evidence also survives in the limestone caves of Dire Dawa, which contain stone hand tools, blade instruments and drawings.

A French archaeological team discovered the Laas Geel cave paintings in November and December 2002 while searching Somaliland for sites documenting the historical period when production economy appeared. The paintings depict long-horned cattle wearing ceremonial robes, their necks embellished with a plastron-like decoration.

Dhagah Kureh, whose name translates to 'the stone with the head,' is a rock shelter site in Somaliland formed from stony outcrops along a roughly 4 km-long granite range. Its Shelter 1 holds the greatest number of rock art panels depicting large cows found anywhere in Somaliland.

The Dhambalin paintings include hunting scenes with eight to ten people shown carrying bows and arrows, surrounded by wildlife such as antelopes and dogs. One hunter is depicted with hair down and headgear, accompanied by two dogs, while another appears to sit on an animal, possibly a horse.

Besides the long-horned decorated cattle, the Laas Geel rock art also includes an image of a domesticated dog, several depictions of other Canidae, and a giraffe. The site's excellent preservation is credited to granite overhangs that shelter the paintings from the elements.

The earliest development of both the wavy-line and dotted wavy-line potteries dates to the 8th millennium BCE. It took place at Sagai and Sarurab in Sudan, from where the styles later spread across the Saharan-Sahelian region.

Among the Dhambalin paintings is a humanoid figure rendered in white with a head unusually large compared to its body, possibly representing a child. Throughout the site, human figures are painted less lifelike than the animals surrounding them.

war.text: Nataruk, in Turkana County, Kenya, is a site where archaeologists found the remains of 27 people (6 young children, 1 teenager and 20 adults) dating between 9,500 and 10,500 years ago. Researchers led by Marta Mirazón Lahr interpreted it as a "massacre": the adults and six children showed signs of a violent end, having been clubbed or stabbed and left to die without burial. They called it the earliest known evidence of intergroup violence among hunter-gatherers.

Ten of the 12 best-preserved skeletons at Nataruk show violent injuries to the head, neck, ribs, hands and knees. These include sharp-force cuts to the neck, blunt or sharp-force blows to the head, crushed knees and ribs, and broken hands, possibly from parrying a blow. The wounds came from at least three kinds of weapons: stone-tipped and sharpened arrows, a club-like weapon, and another close-range weapon, possibly a club or wooden handle with hafted sharp stone blades that caused deep cuts.

Two of the male skeletons at Nataruk had stone projectile tips lodged in the skull and thorax. One tip was still embedded in the side of a skull. Two individuals had no injuries on the bones that survived, but the position of their hands suggests they may have been bound, including a young woman who was heavily pregnant at the time.

About 10,000 years ago the Turkana region was lush and fertile, and Lake Turkana was much larger than it is today. Nataruk itself was a temporary camp where a band of hunter-gatherers came to fish and hunt.

The Nataruk remains were dated using three separate methods: radiocarbon dating by Rachel Wood, optically stimulated luminescence by Jean-Luc Schwenninger, and Uranium-series dating by Rainer Grün. All three methods placed the remains at between 9,500 and 10,500 years old.

Not all researchers accept the massacre interpretation of Nataruk: Christopher Stojanowski argued that much of the skeletal damage may have occurred after the bodies were deposited rather than during a violent attack. He also disputed how the site itself had formed.

General studies of clubs as weapons cite Nataruk in Turkana, Kenya, as one of several historical examples of blunt-force trauma caused by a club. There, such wounds occurred during a prehistoric conflict between bands of hunter-gatherers about 10,000 years ago.

literature.text: At Dhagah Nabi Galay, part of the Laas Geel complex in Somaliland, rock art includes what is considered the first examples of writing in East Africa. It is believed to have been developed by a Neolithic civilization in northern Somalia, offering a rare glimpse of the region before Islam arrived.

Dhagah Nabi Galay, a site associated with the Laas Geel complex near Hargeisa, features what is considered the first examples of writing in East Africa. Its rock art includes a script believed to have been developed by a Neolithic civilization in northern Somalia, though little research has been done on it.

science.text: Between about 5,000 and 7,000 years ago, people in the Horn of Africa domesticated the donkey from the region's Nubian and Somalian wild ass populations. Genetic evidence shows that Cushitic-speaking peoples in the Horn of Africa and along the Red Sea Hills domesticated the animal separately from other groups, boosting the mobility of pastoral communities.

Sorghum, now the world's fifth-most important cereal crop, was domesticated from its wild ancestor more than 5,000 years ago in eastern Sudan, in the area of the Atbara and Gash rivers. Its origins lie among some of the earliest farming communities in the region.

By about 5,000 years ago, communities in what is now Kenya and Tanzania had begun herding livestock and making pottery, marking the start of the Pastoral Neolithic. Unlike Neolithic societies elsewhere that turned to farming, this first African food-production system was built on nomadic pastoralism.

In Ethiopia, cultivation of enset, sometimes called the false banana, is reported to date back 10,000 years, placing its earliest use at the very start of this era. There is, however, little empirical evidence to confirm so early a date.

Archaeologists have found sorghum remains near Kassala in eastern Sudan dating from 3500 to 3000 BCE, associated with the Neolithic Butana Group culture. This is some of the earliest direct evidence for a crop that would go on to feed much of the world.

The spread of herding into East Africa followed the drying of the Sahara. Hunter-gatherers there first adopted livestock such as cattle, sheep and goats in the eighth to seventh millennia BP, and as the Green Sahara's grasslands dried, pastoralism moved southward into the region.

At Laas Geel near Hargeisa in Somaliland, rock art dated to as much as 5,500 years old depicts domesticated African aurochs alongside the herders believed to have created the paintings. These are among the earliest known images of domestic cattle in the Horn of Africa.

At the Dhambalin rock shelter in Somaliland, dated to about 5,000 years ago, paintings show horned cattle, goats, giraffes and sheep, including the earliest known pictures of sheep in Somaliland. Giraffes shown in the art are no longer found in the country today.

The Pastoral Neolithic era in East Africa, which began with herding and pottery by about 5,000 years ago, also saw the construction of megalithic sites. One example is the Jarigole pillar site near Lake Turkana in Kenya.

The domestication of the donkey in the Horn of Africa came well after cattle, sheep and goats had already been domesticated in the seventh and eighth millennia BC. Donkeys further boosted herders' mobility, since, unlike ruminants, they did not need time to chew their cud.

politics.text: Omotic speakers in southwest Ethiopia are known for their ritual monarchy. They also practiced hoe cultivation of cereal grains and tubers.

Around 3800 to 3000 BCE, the Butana Group lived east of the Atbara River. Its society is thought to have had three levels of social hierarchy. This is one of the earliest signs of ranked social organization in the Horn of Africa region.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: The Eastern Cushites lived southwest of the Great Rift Valley, and their dialects were split among two dozen tribes. Along with neighboring people in northern Kenya, they are known for distinct social organization systems. In these systems, classes were recruited through a fixed cycle of grades and intervals.

The only evidence of social complexity in the Butana Group is porphyry mace-heads. Elsewhere in prehistoric Egypt and Nubia, such objects were associated with wealthy burials. Since porphyry was likely imported 300 kilometres to the northeast, some individuals may have had more prestige and authority than others.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: Omotic society is considered the most diversified in the region, divided into fifty subgroups with distinct languages and cultures. The same Omotic speakers are known for their ritual monarchy.

The Atbai tradition, an early culture of the Eritrean-Sudanese lowlands, dates to the 5th millennium BCE. It likely originated in the northern Mereb (Gash) delta. It came long before the Butana Group and the region's later social complexity.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: The Butana Group, Gash Group, and Jebel Mokram Group appear to mark the rise and decline of social complexity between the Atbarah River and the Mereb Delta. The pastoral Gash Group and agropastoral Jebel Mokram Group moved seasonally to the Eritrean-Ethiopian highlands. These movements were a significant part of the regional network.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

politics.text: Egyptian trade with the elusive Land of Punt likely stimulated development in the Eritrean-Sudanese lowlands. This suggests that the rise of ranked societies there was linked to trade with a powerful neighbor far to the north.
politics.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

culture.text: Prehistoric finds at Laas Geel in the Horn of Africa are seen as suggesting a belief system of panentheistic polytheism and naturalistic pantheism. It included the worship of cattle. The later Waaqism of the proto-Somalis appears to leave no traces of such worship.

Around 9000 BC, during the Late Stone Age, Greater Ethiopia had at least two bladelet-making cultures. The Wilton culture made small stone blades, while the Hargeistan culture made long bladelets from obsidian.

The oldest evidence of burial customs in the Horn of Africa comes from cemeteries in Somaliland, dating back to the 4th millennium BCE. This burial evidence sits alongside the pastoral rock art created by early Somaliland shepherds during the same broad Neolithic period.

The Atbai tradition was an early culture of the Eritrean-Sudanese lowlands, dating to the 5th millennium BCE. It likely originated in the northern Mereb (Gash) delta. Egyptian trade with the elusive Land of Punt likely stimulated its development.
culture.source_title: Sabaeans in the Horn of Africa

culture.text: Donald N. Levine held that Proto-Cushitic was spoken on the Ethiopian Highlands by 5000-4000 BC. Cushitic languages are still spoken today, mainly in the Horn of Africa.

The Butana Group lived east of the Atbara River around 3800-3000 BCE. It left porphyry mace-heads, which were linked to wealthy burials in prehistoric Egypt and Nubia. The porphyry was likely imported from 300 kilometres to the northeast, suggesting some individuals held more prestige and authority, within perhaps three levels of social hierarchy.

culture.text: The split between proto-Cushitic and proto-Omotic began by the fourth or fifth millennium BC. Linguistic and cultural fission of the proto-Ethiopians followed. Later, they were classified into five stable groups.
